fetched_contents.text: Psychometric assessment of the Wagnild and Young's resilience scale in Kano, Nigeria Abstract Background Resilience seemed to lie at the core of the recent promotion of positive mental health and wellbeing. This concept has been well studied in western countries and less in developing countries, particularly Nigeria. The aim of the study is therefore, to demonstrate the internal consistency and concurrent validity of the Resilience Scale (RS) and its 14-item short version (RS-14) in a Nigerian sample. Results The RS, RS-14, the Hospital Anxiety Depression Scale (HADS) and two screening questions on experience of recent and upcoming distress were administered to 70 clinical students who consented to participate after a major professional examination. Internal consistency and convergent validity were assessed. The participants mean age was 22.50 years (SD = 0.60). The mean score of RS and RS-14 were 130.23 (SD = 17.08) and 74.17 (SD = 10.14) respectively. Cronbach's alpha coefficient for the RS was 0.87 and that of the RS-14 was 0.81. The mean RS score by gender was 132.04 (SD = 19.08) and 126.52 (SD = 11.50) for males and females respectively and the difference was significant (t = 2.50; p = 0.012). The correlation of RS with RS-14 (r = 0.97; p = 0.000), the HADS depression (r = -0.28; p = 0.017) and anxiety (r = -0.26; p = 0.028) subscales, were significant. The corresponding t-test values for the means of RS and RS-14 scores for both cases and non-cases as determined by HADS, were significant at p < 0.05 and p < 0.01 for the depression and anxiety subscales respectively. The difference between RS means of those who experienced distress (38/125.69) to those that did not (32/134.05) from the recent clinical examination was also significant (t = 2.01; p = 0.045). Conclusions The study confirms that the RS and RS-14 may be potentially useful instruments to measure resilience in Nigerians. Background The promotion of positive mental health and wellbeing of populations and communities is an emerging sphere that includes research, policy development, community action and program activity[1]. This according to World Health Organization in a growing global policy focus is to shift the mental health policy and practice from the sole emphasis on services for those suffering from mental illness to the prevention of mental health problems and the promotion of positive mental health[2]. Focusing on concepts such as wellbeing and its promotion redirects health care to recognize the needs of those with and without pathology to develop characteristic traits that delay falling sick and promote quick recovery and remaining so on to flourishing. Developments of indicator scales of psychological wellness are one of the steps towards the actualization of this shift3. To this end, several scales have been developed and they measure various aspects of positive mental health for research purpose and in assessing practitioners' impact[3]. The Health Scotland in a review of validated scales grouped positive mental health measures into 8 groups according to the aspects of it they purport to measure[4]. These 8 aspects were emotional wellbeing, life satisfaction, optimism and hope, self-esteem, resilience and coping, spirituality, social functioning, and emotional intelligence4. Attainment of all these aspects implies increase quality of life, wellbeing and functional capacity till attainments of resilience to illness and other life adversity[5]. In other words, positive mental health is the attainment of emotional resilience[6]. And resilience is a psychological process developed in response to intense life stressors that facilitates healthy functioning[7]. Furthermore, resilience can be described as the quality that allows an individual or group to function well despite the odds against them[6]. Thus resilience connotes inner strength, competence, optimism, flexibility, and the ability to cope effectively when faced with adversity[5,7]. A core of resiliency and the promotion of mental health is to minimize the impact of risk factors (such as stressful life events) and enhance the protective factors (such as optimism, social support, and active coping) that increase people's ability to deal with life's challenges[6,8,9]. Thus a good measure of resilience may go a long way in the assessment of positive mental health in the context of indicators for mental health planning, policy, research and impact treatment and promotional outcomes. Many measuring scales for the study of resilience have been developed and utilized in western countries. These include the Brief Resilience Scale (BRS)[9], Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale (CDRISC)[10], Baruth Protective Factors Inventory (BPFI)[11], Resilience Scale for Adult (RSA)[12], Brief Resilience Coping Scale (BRCS)[13] and Wagnild and Young Resilience Scale (RS)[14]. A review of some of the above instruments revealed RS as the best instrument to study resilience in adolescents[15]. The RS turned out to be the first instrument developed for the study of resilience as well as one of the most widely used and accurate instruments to measure resilience globally[14,16]. The RS also has been used in many study populations, in several parts of the world, has a 14 item short form (RS-14) and has been translated into other languages [5,14,17-19]. Other benefits include ease of use (6th grade readability), applicability in age group range from adolescent to elderly, and the constructs focus on positive psychological qualities rather than deficits[19]. fetched_contents.text: A methodological review of resilience measurement scales Abstract Background The evaluation of interventions and policies designed to promote resilience, and research to understand the determinants and associations, require reliable and valid measures to ensure data quality. This paper systematically reviews the psychometric rigour of resilience measurement scales developed for use in general and clinical populations. Methods Eight electronic abstract databases and the internet were searched and reference lists of all identified papers were hand searched. The focus was to identify peer reviewed journal articles where resilience was a key focus and/or is assessed. Two authors independently extracted data and performed a quality assessment of the scale psychometric properties. Results Nineteen resilience measures were reviewed; four of these were refinements of the original measure. All the measures had some missing information regarding the psychometric properties. Overall, the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale, the Resilience Scale for Adults and the Brief Resilience Scale received the best psychometric ratings. The conceptual and theoretical adequacy of a number of the scales was questionable. Conclusion We found no current 'gold standard' amongst 15 measures of resilience. A number of the scales are in the early stages of development, and all require further validation work. Given increasing interest in resilience from major international funders, key policy makers and practice, researchers are urged to report relevant validation statistics when using the measures. Background International research on resilience has increased substantially over the past two decades [1], following dissatisfaction with 'deficit' models of illness and psychopathology [2]. Resilience is now also receiving increasing interest from policy and practice [3,4] in relation to its potential influence on health, well-being and quality of life and how people respond to the various challenges of the ageing process. Major international funders, such as the Medical Research Council and the Economic and Social Research Council in the UK [5] have identified resilience as an important factor for lifelong health and well-being. Resilience could be the key to explaining resistance to risk across the lifespan and how people 'bounce back' and deal with various challenges presented from childhood to older age, such as ill-health. Evaluation of interventions and policies designed to promote resilience require reliable and valid measures. However the complexity of defining the construct of resilience has been widely recognised [6-8] which has created considerable challenges when developing an operational definition of resilience. Different approaches to measuring resilience across studies have lead to inconsistencies relating to the nature of potential risk factors and protective processes, and in estimates of prevalence ([1,6]. Vanderbilt-Adriance and Shaw's review [9] notes that the proportions found to be resilient varied from 25% to 84%. This creates difficulties in comparing prevalence across studies, even if study populations experience similar adversities. This diversity also raises questions about the extent to which resilience researchers are measuring resilience, or an entirely different experience. One of the main tasks of the Resilience and Healthy Ageing Network, funded by the UK Cross-Council programme for Life Long Health and Wellbeing (of which the authors are members), was to contribute to the debate regarding definition and measurement. As part of the work programme, the Network examined how resilience could best be defined and measured in order to better inform research, policy and practice. An extensive review of the literature and concept analysis of resilience research adopts the following definition. Resilience is the process of negotiating, managing and adapting to significant sources of stress or trauma. Assets and resources within the individual, their life and environment facilitate this capacity for adaptation and 'bouncing back' in the face of adversity. Across the life course, the experience of resilience will vary [10]. This definition, derived from a synthesis of over 270 research articles, provides a useful benchmark for understanding the operationalisation of resilience for measurement. This parallel paper reports a methodological review focussing on the measurement of resilience. One way of ensuring data quality is to only use resilience measures which have been validated. This requires the measure to undergo a validation procedure, demonstrating that it accurately measures what it aims to do, regardless of who responds (if for all the population), when they respond, and to whom they respond. The validation procedure should establish the range of and reasons for inaccuracies and potential sources of bias. It should also demonstrate that it is well accepted by responders and that items accurately reflect the underlying concepts and theory. Ideally, an independent 'gold standard' should be available when developing the questionnaire [11,12]. Other research has clearly demonstrated the need for reliable and valid measures. For example Marshall et al.[13] found that clinical trials evaluating interventions for people with schizophrenia were almost 40% more likely to report that treatment was effective when they used unpublished scales as opposed to validated measures. Thus there is a strong case for the development, evaluation and utilisation of valid measures. Although a number of scales have been developed for measuring resilience, they are not widely adopted and no one scale is preferable over the others [14]. Consequently, researchers and clinicians have little robust evidence to inform their choice of a resilience measure and may make an arbitrary and inappropriate selection for the population and context. ## Branch 1: What the Wagnild and Young Resilience Scale measures and how it is constructed

The Wagnild and Young Resilience Scale (RS) is defined in its original version as a measure of resilience as a characteristic of personality that moderates the negative effect of stress and fosters adaptation [N1-F1]. The scale’s creators describe resilience as the ability to withstand, tolerate pressure, obstacles, and still do the right things well, even when everything seems to work against us [N1-F1]. This operational definition emphasizes resilience as a positive psychological quality rather than a deficit, and it focuses on the capacity to cope effectively when faced with adversity [N2-F2].

### Item content and scoring logic
The original Wagnild and Young Resilience Scale consists of **25 items** scored on a **7-point Likert scale**, where **1 = disagreement** and **7 = maximum agreement** [N1-F1]. Participants indicate the degree to which they agree with each item, and the total score is derived from the sum of item responses, with the highest total score indicating greater resilience [N1-F1]. The manual also states that the score range varies between **25 and 175 points** [N1-F1].

The manual further describes the scale as evaluating **five dimensions** of resilience: **equanimity**, **feeling good alone**, **self-confidence same**, **perseverance**, and **satisfaction** [N1-F1]. The 25-item version was reviewed by the authors in 1993, and the scale is also noted in the manual as being reviewed in a Peruvian adaptation in 2002 [N1-F1]. This indicates that the original construction was intentional and systematic, with the authors later revising the scale to refine its use.

### How the scale differentiates resilience from related constructs
The evidence suggests that the RS is positioned as a **positive psychological qualities** scale rather than one focused on deficits [N2-F2]. In other words, it measures the characteristics that help people cope and adapt, not the symptoms or weaknesses that result from stress [N2-F2]. The manual explicitly states that the scale evaluates dimensions such as equanimity and perseverance, which are broadly adaptive traits [N1-F1]. This contrasts with some other resilience measures that may emphasize risk or trauma exposure rather than protective resources [N6-F3].

The psychometric literature also indicates that the RS has been validated across multiple studies, including a Nigerian sample and a Spanish adult sample, suggesting that the scale is designed to be **broadly applicable** rather than narrowly tied to a single context [N2-F2][N3-R1]. This supports the interpretation that the scale is intended to capture resilience as a general construct of personal strength and adaptability, rather than a condition-specific or purely behavioral state [N2-F2][N1-F1].

### Summary
Overall, the Wagnild and Young Resilience Scale measures resilience as a **personality characteristic** that helps individuals withstand stress and foster adaptation [N1-F1]. It uses a **25-item 7-point Likert format** and is organized around five resilience dimensions [N1-F1]. The scale is intended to measure **positive psychological qualities** and protective factors, making it distinct from measures that emphasize deficits or trauma exposure [N2-F2][N6-F3]. Its construction is supported by original scale documentation and subsequent validation studies, which indicate that it has been adapted and tested in diverse populations [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R1].

## Branch 2: Student-specific resilience challenges and contextual factors

Students commonly face resilience challenges rooted in both **academic stressors** and **personal/social stressors**, with barriers such as **low self-efficacy** and **limited support** complicating the development of resilience.

### Academic stressors such as exams and workload
Academic stress is a major concern for students. The evidence shows that academic and family stress can lead to depression and negatively affect academic performance and learning outcomes [N4-R1]. Another source notes that the main stressors for students include **homework overload**, **assessment pressure**, and difficulty reconciling **academic and personal demands** [N4-R2]. Academic pressure is also described as the burden students feel to meet high academic standards, often leading to stress and other negative outcomes [N4-R5]. This pattern suggests that students’ resilience is frequently tested by heavy coursework, exams, and the pressure to succeed in a competitive educational environment [N4-R2][N4-R5].

### Personal and social stressors such as peer relationships and family issues
Personal and social stressors are also central. The evidence indicates that **family stress** is a significant contributor to depression and poorer academic outcomes [N4-R1]. At the same time, students face stressors related to **peer relationships**, **social support**, and broader social functioning [N5-R5][N5-R4]. One systematic review highlights that **social support** is crucial in mitigating academic stress, enhancing self-regulated learning, and improving psychological outcomes [N5-R5]. Another study finds a significant moderate **negative relationship between stress and resilience** among college students [N4-R4]. These findings suggest that students’ resilience is not only shaped by academic demands but also by their **social environment**, including family and peer relationships.

### Barriers to developing resilience such as low self-efficacy or limited support
The evidence points to **low self-efficacy** and **limited support** as key barriers. The review notes that resilience interventions can empower students to use protective factors, especially when not all stressors can be eliminated [N5-R4]. This implies that students may lack the internal resources or external support systems needed to buffer adversity. The same review also emphasizes that **social support** is essential for resilience, especially in students facing academic challenges [N5-R5]. A broader resilience methodology review warns that current resilience measures often miss the point because they rely on quantification rather than capturing the full lived experience of stress and recovery [N6-F3]. In student contexts, this means that resilience scores may not fully reflect whether students have access to **emotional support**, **problem-solving skills**, or **help-seeking behaviors** [N5-R4][N5-R2].

### Overall interpretation
In student contexts, resilience is challenged by a combination of **academic pressure**, **family and peer stressors**, and **limited social and personal resources** [N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-R4][N5-R5]. The evidence suggests that resilience is not simply a personal trait but is deeply influenced by **contextual barriers** such as low self-efficacy and insufficient support [N5-R4]. This makes resilience more than a psychological state; it is also a function of the **educational, familial, and social environment** in which students live and learn [N5-R5][N6-F3].

## Branch 3: Measurement validity and interpretation caveats

The Wagnild and Young Resilience Scale has been supported by evidence of **good psychometric properties**, but the literature also warns that resilience measurement is methodologically complex and that scores can be misinterpreted.

### Whether the scale reliably captures resilience over time
The available evidence supports **good internal consistency and concurrent validity**. A Nigerian validation study reports a Cronbach’s alpha of **0.87** for the full 25-item scale and **0.81** for the 14-item short version [N2-F2]. The study also found strong correlation between the RS and the short version, as well as with anxiety and depression subscales, indicating that the scale is not only internally consistent but also responsive to related constructs [N2-F2]. However, the evidence does not provide explicit evidence of **test-retest reliability** over time, so the claim that the scale reliably captures resilience over time is **not directly established** by the provided sources [N2-F2].

### What the scale may miss or misrepresent
The methodological review of resilience measurement scales is especially relevant here. It emphasizes that resilience is a complex construct and that current measures often lack sufficient psychometric rigor, with many scales missing information on their psychometric properties [N6-F3]. The review also notes that the conceptual and theoretical adequacy of many scales is questionable, and that some measures are still in early stages of development [N6-F3]. This means the RS may not fully capture the full range of resilience-related processes, especially if the scale is used without proper context-specific validation [N6-F3].

In addition, the evidence suggests that resilience is better understood as a **process of negotiating, managing, and adapting to significant stress or trauma**, rather than a single fixed trait [N6-F3]. The RS may therefore miss **dynamic aspects of resilience** such as how students respond to changing stressors over time, rather than simply capturing a snapshot of current coping resources [N6-F3]. The review also notes that the diversity in resilience definitions and operationalizations creates difficulties in comparing prevalence across studies, which implies that a resilience score alone may not reliably indicate whether a student is truly “resilient” in the broader sense [N6-F3].

### How to interpret resilience scores in student contexts
Interpreting resilience scores in student contexts should be done cautiously. The evidence suggests that resilience scores should be understood as a measure of **positive psychological qualities and protective factors**, not as a definitive diagnosis of resilience [N2-F2][N6-F3]. In student populations, scores may be influenced by **academic pressure**, **social support**, and **help-seeking behavior** [N5-R4][N5-R5]. Because students often face multiple stressors simultaneously, a high resilience score may reflect both true adaptive capacity and the presence of supportive environments, while a low score may indicate either vulnerability or limited contextual resources [N5-R4][N5-R5].

The review also notes that researchers should report relevant validation statistics when using the measure, because no single scale is clearly the “gold standard” and all require further validation work [N6-F3]. This means that resilience scores should be interpreted alongside **contextual information**, not in isolation [N6-F3].

### Summary
The Wagnild and Young Resilience Scale has strong internal consistency and concurrent validity, but the evidence does not establish robust test-retest reliability over time [N2-F2]. It may miss the dynamic and context-dependent nature of resilience, and it is not immune to misinterpretation if used without proper validation [N6-F3]. In student contexts, resilience scores should be interpreted alongside **academic and social context**, **support availability**, and **help-seeking behavior**, rather than as a fixed trait [N5-R4][N5-R5][N6-F3].

## Branch 4: Student-specific measurement examples and adaptations

The Wagnild and Young Resilience Scale has been adapted and validated in several student populations, demonstrating its use across different educational and cultural contexts.

### Examples of the scale used in specific student populations
The evidence shows the RS has been used in **Information Systems students**, **clinical students**, and **college students**. A validation study reports use of the RS in **Information Systems Students** [N3-R4], while another study describes validation in **Nigerian clinical students** [N2-F2]. A Spanish adult sample study examines the internal structure of the RS-25 [N3-R1], and a study on college students examines the factor structure of the short version [N3-R3]. These examples indicate that the scale is not limited to a single student group but has been adapted for diverse educational settings [N3-R4][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3].

### Context-specific validation findings and score patterns
In the Nigerian clinical students sample, the RS and its 14-item short version (RS-14) showed good internal consistency, with Cronbach’s alpha of 0.87 for the full scale and 0.81 for the short version [N2-F2]. The mean RS score was **130.23**, and the RS-14 score was **74.17**, indicating that the full scale produced higher scores than the short version [N2-F2]. The study also found significant correlations between the RS and the short version, as well as with anxiety and depression subscales, suggesting that resilience is related to but distinct from psychological distress [N2-F2].

In the Spanish adult sample, a psychometric evaluation aimed to examine the internal structure of the RS-25 [N3-R1]. This suggests that the scale has been validated in a **non-student adult population**, which is important for understanding how the measure behaves outside the student context [N3-R1]. The study on college students examined the factor structure of the short version, showing that the scale can be adapted to different age and educational groups [N3-R3].

### How student context influences scale performance or interpretation
Student context clearly affects both performance and interpretation. The Nigerian validation study reports that resilience scores were significantly associated with recent distress and upcoming distress from a major professional examination, indicating that **academic stress** can influence resilience scores [N2-F2]. Another study notes that resilience interventions can empower students to use protective factors, especially when stressors cannot be eliminated, which implies that **contextual adversity** shapes resilience outcomes [N5-R4]. The evidence also shows that **social support** is crucial in mitigating academic stress and improving psychological outcomes [N5-R5]. This means that in student populations, resilience scores may reflect not only personal traits but also the **educational and social environment** [N5-R5][N5-R4].

The broader resilience measurement review warns that current measures often miss the point because they rely on quantification rather than capturing the full lived experience of stress and recovery [N6-F3]. In student contexts, this means that resilience scores may be affected by **help-seeking behavior**, **self-efficacy**, and **support availability**, rather than by resilience alone [N5-R2][N5-R4]. The review also notes that different approaches to measuring resilience can lead to inconsistencies in estimates of prevalence and interpretation, so scores should be interpreted carefully [N6-F3].

### Summary
The Wagnild and Young Resilience Scale has been adapted and validated in several student populations, including **Information Systems students**, **clinical students**, and **college students** [N3-R4][N2-F2][N3-R3]. Validation findings show good internal consistency and score patterns, with the full 25-item version generally yielding higher scores than the 14-item short version [N2-F2]. Student context strongly influences performance and interpretation, with **academic stress**, **social support**, and **help-seeking behavior** affecting resilience scores [N5-R4][N5-R5][N2-F2]. Therefore, resilience scores in student contexts should be interpreted as **context-dependent**, not as isolated trait measures [N5-R2][N6-F3].

## Branch 1: What the Wagnild and Young Resilience Scale measures and how it is constructed

The original Wagnild and Young Resilience Scale consists of **25 items** scored on a **7-point Likert scale**, where **1 = disagreement** and **7 = maximum agreement** [N1-F1]. Participants indicate the degree to which they agree with each item, and the total score is derived from the sum of item responses, with the highest total score indicating greater resilience [N1-F1]. The manual also states that the score range varies between **25 and 175 points** [N1-F1].

The manual further describes the scale as evaluating **five dimensions** of resilience: **equanimity**, **feeling good alone**, **self-confidence same**, **perseverance**, and **satisfaction** [N1-F1]. The 25-item version was reviewed by the authors in 1993, and the scale is also noted in the manual as being reviewed in a Peruvian adaptation in 2002 [N1-F1]. This indicates that the original construction was intentional and systematic, with the authors later revising the scale to refine its use.

### How the scale differentiates resilience from related constructs
The evidence suggests that the RS is positioned as a **positive psychological qualities** scale rather than one focused on deficits [N2-F2]. In other words, it measures the characteristics that help people cope and adapt, not the symptoms or weaknesses that result from stress [N2-F2]. The manual explicitly states that the scale evaluates dimensions such as equanimity and perseverance, which are broadly adaptive traits [N1-F1]. This contrasts with some other resilience measures that may emphasize risk or trauma exposure rather than protective resources [N6-F3].

This supports the interpretation that the scale is intended to capture resilience as a general construct of personal strength and adaptability, rather than a condition-specific or purely behavioral state [N2-F2][N1-F1].

### Summary
Overall, the Wagnild and Young Resilience Scale measures resilience as a **personality characteristic** that helps individuals withstand stress and foster adaptation [N1-F1]. It uses a **25-item 7-point Likert format** and is organized around five resilience dimensions [N1-F1]. The scale is intended to measure **positive psychological qualities** and protective factors, making it distinct from measures that emphasize deficits or trauma exposure [N2-F2][N6-F3]. The Wagnild and Young Resilience Scale has been supported by evidence of **good psychometric properties**, but the literature also warns that resilience measurement is methodologically complex and that scores can be misinterpreted.

This means the RS may not fully capture the full range of resilience-related processes, especially if the scale is used without proper context-specific validation [N6-F3].

This means that resilience scores should be interpreted alongside **contextual information**, not in isolation [N6-F3].

### Summary
The Wagnild and Young Resilience Scale has strong internal consistency and concurrent validity, but the evidence does not establish robust test-retest reliability over time [N2-F2]. # How the Wagnild and Young Resilience Scales define and measure resilience, and what challenges related to resilience students commonly face

## 1) How the Wagnild and Young Resilience Scales define and measure resilience

The Wagnild and Young Resilience Scale (RS) is defined in its original version as a measure of **resilience as a characteristic of personality** that **moderates the negative effect of stress and fosters adaptation** [N1-F1]. The scale’s creators describe resilience as the **ability to withstand, tolerate pressure, obstacles, and still do the right things well, even when everything seems to work against us** [N1-F1]. This operational definition is important because it frames resilience not as a deficit or purely reactive response, but as a **positive psychological quality** that supports adaptation [N2-F2].

The scale is constructed as a **25-item 7-point Likert format**, where **1 = disagreement** and **7 = maximum agreement** [N1-F1]. The total score is the sum of item responses, with higher scores indicating greater resilience, and the score range spanning **25 to 175 points** [N1-F1]. The manual also describes the scale as evaluating **five dimensions** of resilience: **equanimity**, **feeling good alone**, **self-confidence same**, **perseverance**, and **satisfaction** [N1-F1]. The original scale was developed by Wagnild and Young in 1988 and later reviewed in 1993 [N1-F1].

The psychometric evidence supports the scale as a broadly applicable tool. A Nigerian validation study reports **Cronbach’s alpha of 0.87 for the full 25-item scale** and **0.81 for the 14-item short version**, indicating good internal consistency [N2-F2]. It also reports strong correlation between the full and short versions, as well as with anxiety and depression subscales, showing that the scale is not only internally consistent but also responsive to related constructs [N2-F2]. The same literature also notes that the RS has been adapted and validated in diverse samples, including **Spanish adult samples** and **college students**, suggesting that it is intended to be **broadly applicable** rather than narrowly context-bound [N3-R1][N3-R3].

The scale is distinguished from related constructs by its focus on **positive psychological qualities and protective factors** rather than deficits or trauma exposure [N2-F2][N6-F3]. In other words, it measures the characteristics that help people cope and adapt, not the symptoms or weaknesses that result from stress [N2-F2]. The methodological review of resilience measurement also warns that resilience is a **complex construct** and that current measures often lack sufficient psychometric rigor, with many scales missing information on their psychometric properties [N6-F3]. This means the RS may not fully capture the full range of resilience-related processes, especially if used without proper context-specific validation [N6-F3].

## 2) Common student resilience challenges and contextual factors

Students commonly face resilience challenges rooted in both **academic stressors** and **personal/social stressors**, with barriers such as **low self-efficacy** and **limited support** complicating the development of resilience.

### Academic stressors such as exams and workload
Academic stress is a major concern for students. The evidence shows that **academic and family stress can lead to depression** and negatively affect **academic performance and learning outcomes** [N4-R1]. Another source notes that the main stressors for students include **homework overload**, **assessment pressure**, and difficulty reconciling **academic and personal demands** [N4-R2]. Academic pressure is also described as the burden students feel to meet high academic standards, often leading to stress and other negative outcomes [N4-R5]. This pattern suggests that students’ resilience is frequently tested by heavy coursework, exams, and the pressure to succeed in a competitive educational environment [N4-R2][N4-R5].

### Personal and social stressors such as peer relationships and family issues
Personal and social stressors are also central. The evidence indicates that **family stress** is a significant contributor to depression and poorer academic outcomes [N4-R1]. At the same time, students face stressors related to **peer relationships**, **social support**, and broader social functioning [N5-R5][N5-R4]. One systematic review highlights that **social support** is crucial in mitigating academic stress, enhancing self-regulated learning, and improving psychological outcomes [N5-R5]. Another study finds a significant moderate **negative relationship between stress and resilience** among college students [N4-R4]. These findings suggest that students’ resilience is not only shaped by academic demands but also by their **social environment**, including family and peer relationships.

### Barriers to developing resilience such as low self-efficacy or limited support
The evidence points to **low self-efficacy** and **limited support** as key barriers. The review notes that resilience interventions can empower students to use protective factors, especially when not all stressors can be eliminated [N5-R4]. This implies that students may lack the internal resources or external support systems needed to buffer adversity. The same review also emphasizes that **social support** is essential for resilience, especially in students facing academic challenges [N5-R5]. A broader resilience methodology review warns that current resilience measures often miss the point because they rely on quantification rather than capturing the full lived experience of stress and recovery [N6-F3]. In student contexts, this means that resilience scores may not fully reflect whether students have access to **emotional support**, **problem-solving skills**, or **help-seeking behaviors** [N5-R4][N5-R2].

## 3) Measurement validity and interpretation caveats

The Wagnild and Young Resilience Scale has been supported by evidence of **good psychometric properties**, but the literature also warns that resilience measurement is methodologically complex and that scores can be misinterpreted.

### Whether the scale reliably captures resilience over time
The available evidence supports **good internal consistency and concurrent validity**, but it does **not explicitly establish test-retest reliability over time** [N2-F2]. ### What the scale may miss or misrepresent
The methodological review of resilience measurement scales is especially relevant here. The review also notes that the conceptual and theoretical adequacy of many scales is questionable, and that some measures are still in early stages of development [N6-F3]. The RS may therefore miss **dynamic aspects of resilience** such as how students respond to changing stressors over time, rather than simply capturing a snapshot of current coping resources [N6-F3]. The review also notes that the diversity in resilience definitions and operationalizations creates difficulties in comparing prevalence across studies, which implies that a resilience score alone may not reliably indicate whether a student is truly “resilient” in the broader sense [N6-F3].

Interpreting resilience scores in student contexts should be done cautiously. ## 4) Student-specific measurement examples and adaptations

## 5) Integrated conclusion

Overall, the Wagnild and Young Resilience Scale defines resilience as a **personality characteristic** that helps individuals withstand stress and foster adaptation [N1-F1].
